headline: A strong cold front brings windy, rainy weather and dangerous surf tonight, with more wet systems next week.
summary:
Today (Saturday) is mild, with highs near 60. Rain starts along the coast this afternoon but is not expected to reach the Puget Sound area by late afternoon. A strong cold front arrives from the ocean this evening. It reaches the coast in the evening, crosses the Puget Sound area around midnight, and gets into the Cascades by early Sunday morning. Forecasters say this front "has some punch." They expect southerly gusts as high as 60 mph on the northern and Grays Harbor coasts. Gusts of 45 to 50 mph are expected tonight into early Sunday morning across the interior from Seattle northward, including the San Juan Islands, and along the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Admiralty Inlet. Many leaves are still on the trees, which raises the chance of impacts even from winds near advisory strength.

Ocean seas are forecast to rise quickly to 22 to 26 feet along the beaches tonight and stay that high through Sunday. Forecasters say this, combined with the strong winds, makes conditions dangerous for the clam dig. Sunday brings a quick calm-down. It will still be breezy in the morning, but showers will be minimal and mostly done by noon. Highs will be in the mid 50s under mostly cloudy skies.

The pattern stays active and mild next week. A weaker system arrives Monday, with rain reaching the coast in the afternoon and possibly the inland lowlands by late afternoon. Forecasters say it will not produce winds like tonight's. More fronts follow Monday night and Tuesday, and an atmospheric river (a narrow stream of moist air) sets up around Tuesday night, with most of its moisture aimed at Vancouver Island. Wednesday could be close to record warm in some places. Another system arrives Friday with rain likely inland and cooler highs in the mid 50s. River flooding is not expected over the next seven days, but repeated rain will soak the ground, which could become a concern with storms late next week.

timeline.what: Mild, with highs near 60. Rain develops along the coast in the afternoon but is not expected to reach the Puget Sound area by late afternoon. Winds pick up on the coast late in the afternoon.

The cold front reaches the coast in the evening, moves through the Puget Sound area around midnight, and is into the Cascades by early Sunday morning. Rain and strong southerly winds come with it. Gusts reach up to 60 mph on the coast and 45 to 50 mph in the interior zones under advisory. Ocean seas rise to 22 to 26 feet, and the high surf warning begins at 10 PM.

Breezy in the morning, then calmer. Few showers, mostly over by noon. Highs in the mid 50s with mostly cloudy skies. Seas stay at 22 to 26 feet, easing overnight. Lows are in the mid 30s to mid 40s. The high surf warning ends at 10 PM Sunday.

The next front is still offshore late Monday afternoon. Rain reaches the coast in the afternoon, with a chance of rain inland by late afternoon. Winds are weaker than tonight's. The front moves through Monday night, with another right behind it.

Wet and mild. An atmospheric river sets up around Tuesday night, with most moisture aimed at Vancouver Island. Highs are near 60 Tuesday and Thursday and in the lower to mid 60s Wednesday. Wednesday could be close to record highs; the forecast for Seattle is 64, against a record of 65 set in 1990. Rain is only a chance on Wednesday and Thursday, mainly along the coast.
Another system moves in from the Pacific. Rain is likely inland, and highs drop back to the mid 50s.

confidence: Forecasters are confident about tonight's strong front, enough to upgrade the high wind watch to a warning and add wind advisories. They also say models agree well on the Monday night and Tuesday fronts and on Friday's system. They are much less sure about Wednesday and Thursday, because models disagree on whether the trailing cold front stalls near the coast or farther offshore, and whether it moves through at all Thursday. That is why rain chances for those days are only "chance."
hazards: High Wind Warning for the Grays Harbor County Coast and Northern Washington Coast, 4 PM today to 4 AM Sunday, with southerly gusts as high as 60 mph.

Wind Advisory, 6 PM today to 4 AM Sunday, for Seattle, Everett/Marysville, the Eastside, Island County, the Pierce and southern King County lowlands, the western Skagit, northwestern Snohomish and western Whatcom lowlands, Port Townsend, San Juan County, and the Shoreline/Lynnwood/south Everett area. Gusts of 45 to 50 mph are expected.

Wind Advisory, 4 PM today to 4 AM Sunday, for the Olympic Peninsula foothills, the Lake Crescent area including US 101, the Lower and Middle Chehalis River Valley, the western Strait of Juan de Fuca, and the Willapa and Black Hills.
High Surf Warning, 10 PM tonight to 10 PM Sunday, for the Grays Harbor County Coast and Northern Washington Coast, with seas of 22 to 26 feet. Forecasters call conditions dangerous for the clam dig.

Marine warnings for boaters: Storm Warnings for the ocean coastal waters, and Gale Warnings for the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Admiralty Inlet, the northern inland waters including the San Juan Islands, Puget Sound, and Hood Canal. These run from today into Sunday morning.

glossary.definition: The leading edge of a colder air mass. Its passage often brings a burst of rain and a shift and increase in wind.
The area between a warm front and a cold front, where the air is mild and moist. Western Washington is in it today, which is why it feels mild.
A long, narrow stream of very moist air that can bring prolonged heavy rain when it moves over land. This one is expected to aim mostly at Vancouver Island.
Wind speeds a few thousand feet above the ground, as computer models predict them. Forecasters use them to judge how strong gusts could get at the surface when that wind mixes down.
Scattered showers that follow a front after the main band of rain has passed.
A dip in the high-altitude winds that helps steer storm systems. Here, one digging south offshore on Wednesday would push the warm front north into British Columbia.
A front that stops moving. Forecasters are unsure whether this one stalls along the coast or farther offshore Wednesday and Thursday.
Short for chance of precipitation. The term means rain is possible but not certain, as in the forecast for Wednesday and Thursday.
